'''Gil Kalai''' ({{Langx|he|גיל קלעי}}; born 1955) is an Israeli mathematician and computer scientist. He is the Henry and Manya Noskwith Professor Emeritus of [[Mathematics]] at the [[Hebrew University of Jerusalem]], professor of computer science at the [[Herzliya Interdisciplinary Center|Interdisciplinary Center, Herzliya]], and adjunct professor of mathematics and of computer science at [[Yale University]], United States.<ref name="yale" />

==Biography==
Kalai was born in 1955 in [[Tel Aviv]].<ref name="b723">{{cite web | last1=Hasani | first1=Ilire | last2=Hoffmann | first2=Robert | title=Academy of Europe: CV | website=Academy of Europe | url=https://www.ae-info.org/ae/Member/Kalai_Gil/CV }}</ref> He is the son of [[Hanoch Kalai]], who was a leader of [[Irgun]] and co-founder of [[Lehi (militant group)|Lehi]]. He received his PhD from Hebrew University in 1983 advised by [[Micha Perles]],<ref>{{MathGenealogy|name=Gil Kalai|id=62336}}.</ref> and held a postdoctoral position at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]].<ref name="tue">[http://www.win.tue.nl/math/eidma/courses/minicourses/kalai/MC-DAG-7.html Profile at the Technical University of Eindhoven] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090713111257/http://www.win.tue.nl/math/eidma/courses/minicourses/kalai/MC-DAG-7.html |date=2009-07-13 }} as an instructor of a minicourse on polyhedral combinatorics.</ref> He joined the Hebrew University faculty in 1985, where he has remained since.

From 1995 to 2001, he was the editor-in-chief of the ''[[Israel Journal of Mathematics]]''. In 2016, he was elected honorary member of the [[Hungarian Academy of Sciences]].<ref>{{cite web|title=A Magyar Tudományos Akadémia újonnan megválasztott tagjai (The newly elected members of the Hungarian Academy of Sciences)|website=Magyar Tudományos Akadémia (mta.hu)|date=2 May 2016|url=http://mta.hu/kozgyules2016/a-magyar-tudomanyos-akademia-ujonnan-megvalasztott-tagjai-106411|access-date=2 May 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160505182233/http://mta.hu/kozgyules2016/a-magyar-tudomanyos-akademia-ujonnan-megvalasztott-tagjai-106411|archive-date=5 May 2016|url-status=dead}}</ref> In 2018 he was a plenary speaker with talk ''Noise Stability, Noise Sensitivity and the Quantum Computer Puzzle'' at the [[International Congress of Mathematicians]] in Rio de Janeiro.

==Research==
Kalai is known for finding variants of the [[simplex algorithm]] in [[linear programming]] that can be proven to run in subexponential time,<ref>{{citation|first=Gil|last=Kalai|contribution=A subexponential randomized simplex algorithm|title=Proc. 24th ACM Symp. Theory of Computing (STOC 1992)|year=1992|pages=475–482}}.</ref> for showing that every [[Hereditary property|monotone property of graphs]] has a sharp [[phase transition]],<ref>{{citation|doi=10.1090/S0002-9939-96-03732-X|first1=Ehud|last1=Friedgut|first2=Gil|last2=Kalai|title=Every monotone graph property has a sharp threshold|journal=[[Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society]]|volume=124|year=1996|issue=10|pages=2993–3002|url=https://www.ams.org/proc/1996-124-10/S0002-9939-96-03732-X/|doi-access=free}}.</ref> for solving [[Borsuk's conjecture|Borsuk's problem]] on the number of pieces needed to partition convex sets into subsets of smaller diameter,<ref>{{citation|doi=10.1090/S0273-0979-1993-00398-7|first1=Jeff|last1=Kahn|first2=Gil|last2=Kalai |author-link1=Jeff Kahn (mathematician)|arxiv=math.MG/9307229 |title=A counterexample to Borsuk's conjecture|journal=[[Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society]]|volume=29|year=1993|pages=60–62|s2cid=119647518}}.</ref> and for his work on the [[Hirsch conjecture]] on the diameter of [[convex polytope]]s and in [[polyhedral combinatorics]] more generally.<ref name="kk">{{citation|doi=10.1090/S0273-0979-1992-00285-9|first1=Gil|last1=Kalai|first2=Daniel J.|last2=Kleitman|authorlink2=Daniel Kleitman|title=A quasi-polynomial bound for the diameter of graphs of polyhedra|journal=Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society|volume=26|year=1992|issue=2|pages=315–316|url=https://www.ams.org/bull/1992-26-02/S0273-0979-1992-00285-9/|arxiv=math/9204233|bibcode=1992math......4233K|s2cid=37821778}}.</ref>

===Quantum computing skepticism and conjectures===
Kalai is a noted skeptic of [[quantum computing]] and argues that true quantum computing, which would give exponential speedups over classical computing, cannot be achieved because of inherent limitations when trying to implement [[quantum error correction]] experimentally. He has engaged in a series of public debates with quantum computing researcher [[Aram Harrow]] on his blog,<ref name="i700">{{cite web | title=My Quantum Debate with Aram Harrow: Timeline, Non-technical Highlights, and Flashbacks I | website=Combinatorics and more | date=2013-03-16 | url=https://gilkalai.wordpress.com/2013/03/16/my-quantum-debate-with-aram-harrow-timeline-non-technical-highlights-and-flashbacks-i/ }}</ref><ref name="x857">{{cite web | title=My Quantum Debate with Aram II | website=Combinatorics and more | date=2013-03-19 | url=https://gilkalai.wordpress.com/2013/03/19/my-quantum-debate-with-aram-ii/ }}</ref><ref name="w529">{{cite web | title=My Quantum Debate with Aram III | website=Combinatorics and more | date=2013-03-25 | url=https://gilkalai.wordpress.com/2013/03/25/my-quantum-debate-with-aram-iii/ }}</ref> and has formalized his argument by stating a series of conjectures.<ref name="p643">{{cite web | title=Perpetual Motion of The 21st Century? | website=Gödel&#039;s Lost Letter and P=NP | date=2012-01-30 | url=https://rjlipton.com/2012/01/30/perpetual-motion-of-the-21st-century/ | access-date=2025-11-21}}</ref> Harrow and Steven Flammia published a preprint on [[arXiv]] in 2012 claiming to refute Kalai's Conjecture C,<ref name="a422">{{cite journal | last1=Flammia | first1=Steven T. | last2=Harrow | first2=Aram W. | title=Counterexamples to Kalai's Conjecture C | date=2013 |journal=Q. Inf. & Comp. |volume=13 |issue=1–2 |pages=1–8 | doi=10.26421/QIC13.1-2.0001 | doi-broken-date=29 January 2026 | arxiv=1204.3404 }}</ref> although Kalai later argued in 2022 that there were flaws in their argument.<ref name="q340">{{cite arXiv | last=Kalai | first=Gil | title=Conjecture C Still Stands | date=2022-09-04 | class=quant-ph | eprint=2209.01648 }}</ref> In 2025, Kalai publicly debated quantum computing researcher Matthias Christandl at the [[Learned Society of the Czech Republic]] on whether true quantum computing had already been achieved.<ref name="x094">{{cite web | title=Quantum Duel: Quantum computers – Do they exist? (20 May, 2025) | website=The Learned Society of the Czech Republic | date=2025-05-20 | url=https://www.learned.cz/en/activities/news/quantum-duel-quantum-computers-do-they-exist-20-may-2025.html }}</ref>

Kalai's conjectures are stated as follows:

'''Conjecture 1 (No quantum error correction)'''. The process for creating a quantum error-correcting code will necessarily lead to a mixture of the desired codewords with undesired codewords. The probability of the undesired codewords is uniformly bounded away from zero. (In every implementation of quantum error-correcting codes with one encoded qubit, the probability of not getting the intended qubit is at least some δ > 0, independently of the number of qubits used for encoding.)

'''Conjecture 2'''. A noisy quantum computer is subject to noise in which information leaks for two substantially entangled qubits have a substantial positive correlation.

'''Conjecture 3'''. In any quantum computer at a highly entangled state there will be a strong effect of error-synchronization.

'''Conjecture 4'''. Noisy quantum processes are subject to detrimental noise.<ref>[http://www.ma.huji.ac.il/~kalai/Qitamar.pdf ''How Quantum Computers Fail'' by Gil Kalai (2011)]</ref>{{non-primary source needed|date=October 2024}}

==Recognition==
Kalai was the recipient of the [[Pólya Prize (SIAM)|Pólya Prize]] in 1992, the [[Erdős Prize]] of the Israel Mathematical Society in 1993, and the [[Fulkerson Prize]] in 1994.<ref name="yale">[http://www.cs.yale.edu/people/kalai.html Profile at Yale CS department] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080510144153/http://www.cs.yale.edu/people/kalai.html |date=2008-05-10 }}.</ref> He was also the winner of the 2012 [[Rothschild Prize]] in mathematics.<ref>Yad Hanadiv, [http://www.yadhanadiv.org.il/fellowship-prize/rothschild-prize Rothschild Prize].</ref>  He was named to the 2023 class of Fellows of the [[American Mathematical Society]], "for contributions to combinatorics, convexity, and their applications, as well as to the exposition and communication of mathematics".<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.ams.org/cgi-bin/fellows/fellows_by_year.cgi|title=2023 Class of Fellows|publisher=American Mathematical Society|access-date=2022-11-09|archive-date=2022-11-09|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221109214706/https://www.ams.org/cgi-bin/fellows/fellows_by_year.cgi|url-status=dead}}</ref>
